title: Intuition Gets Stronger the More You Listen to It
author: Jota and Nestor Valles
summary: This essay uses Haruki Murakami's early life to argue that intuition is a faculty strengthened by acting on it, not a flash of certainty that precedes action. It traces his decisions from opening a jazz bar against the advice of everyone he knew, to the moment at a Tokyo baseball game when he thought he could write a novel, to selling a thriving bar to buy two years of writing time. Each step produced a finished thing in the world, whether a business, a prize-winning manuscript or a second book, and each gave him reason to trust the next impulse. The authors stress that no step contained proof of the next, so confidence followed each act rather than preceding it. The practical lesson is that waiting for confidence can keep a person from ever finding it. The piece is based on Murakami's memoir What I Talk About When I Talk About Running.
points: Murakami's path shows that confidence arrived after each act, so waiting to feel sure before deciding can block the very experience that builds trust in your judgment.

His first intuition, to build a life outside conventional employment, required separating the life he wanted from the one others expected, and surviving debt and fatigue proved the conviction was real.
Each completed project, from the bar to the first novel to the second, turned a private hunch into a finished thing in the world and so served as evidence for the next decision.
He twice acted against the unanimous objections of people around him, which suggests that intuition is trained by use rather than by consensus.
The essay frames decisions as a sequence in which every followed intuition leaves a person better able to recognize and trust the next.
quotes: Murakami did not want to become an employee of a conglomerate, a company, or any other organization. But he didn’t imagine himself leading one either.
For an instant, a life presents itself from an angle that had not been visible before. The view is striking.
Opening the jazz bar had required him to distinguish between the life he wanted for himself from the one that others expected of him.
Even if there was not material proof that he could make it as a novelist, Murakami sold the bar against the all too familiar objections of everyone around him.
By the time he gave up the bar, he was not relying on the same intuition he had possessed years earlier. It had been exercised by use.
Running it had taught him that conviction could survive contact with debt and fatigue.
None of these steps gave him certainty about the one that followed. The jazz bar didn’t contain proof of a literary career, and winning a prize didn’t mean that he would become a lasting novelist.
The confidence appeared after each act, not before it. Every intuition he carried into reality left him better able to recognize and trust the next.
